content: Postpartum women are advised to minimize the amount of time they spend being sedentary. Regarding contraception, postpartum women should be provided with appropriate contraceptive options, as recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO). For newborn care, it is essential to assess the baby for danger signs, such as a body temperature below 35.5°C, jaundice within the first 24 hours after birth, or yellow discoloration of the palms and soles at any age. Universal screening for eye abnormalities and hearing impairments is recommended. Early identification of permanent bilateral hearing loss (PBHL) should be conducted using otoacoustic emissions (OAE) or automated auditory brainstem response (AABR). Universal screening for neonatal hyperbilirubinemia is also advised. The use of emollients to prevent skin conditions is not recommended. Clean and dry umbilical cord care is advised, and in specific contexts, the application of chlorhexidine to the umbilical cord stump may be considered to prevent neonatal infections. For safe sleep, placing the infant in a supine position is recommended to reduce the risk of sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS). Immunizations for newborns should follow the latest WHO guidelines for routine vaccinations. Nutritional interventions for newborns include exclusive breastfeeding from birth until six months of age, which is strongly recommended. Vitamin A supplementation for neonates is not recommended, while vitamin D supplementation for breastfed term infants may be considered in specific contexts. Whole-body massage for infants is recommended to support growth and development. Postnatal care should include a minimum of four contacts between healthcare providers and the mother-newborn dyad. If the birth occurs in a healthcare facility, both the mother and newborn should remain under observation for at least 24 hours. If the birth occurs at home, the first postnatal contact should occur within 24 hours. Additional postnatal visits are recommended at 48–72 hours, 7–14 days, and six weeks after birth. These visits should include clinical assessments, timely information, and emotional support provided by skilled and compassionate healthcare workers. Home visits by trained health personnel during the first week after birth are recommended to support the health of both the mother and newborn. Health systems should implement strategies to recruit and retain healthcare workers in rural and remote areas. Policymakers are encouraged to adopt interventions that promote the involvement of men in postnatal care to support maternal and newborn health. Digital tools, such as birth notifications and targeted client communication, may be used in specific contexts to strengthen health systems. The WHO emphasizes the importance of a positive postnatal experience, which includes respectful, individualized, and person-centered care. This care model places the mother and newborn at the center, ensuring their health and well-being during the critical first six weeks after birth. Continuous monitoring, effective referral systems, and high-quality care are essential components of this approach.
